- Wheelbase = 380 (distance between wheel centers, both at same y so centers are on the same horizontal line — good).

Chain: from rear axle (170, 320) to crank (310, 320), radius 10 — chain line from (170+10=180, 320) to (310-10=300, 320) at y=320. Crank radius 30.

Pedal/crank: crank radius 30 (typical is about 170mm, scaled to 30). Pedal position: crank arm from (310, 320): crank arm 1 is (310+30*cosθ, 320+30*sinθ). Pick θ = 45°: cos45≈0.7071 → (331.2, 341.2). The other crank arm at 180°: (288.8, 318.8). Hmm, but a chain should connect the rear wheel and crank. The chain line at y=320 goes from the top of the rear wheel... no wait, in a bicycle the chain wraps around the top of the rear wheel (the drive cog) — actually the chain runs along the top tangent. In a front-view diagram, we draw the chain as a line from the rear wheel hub to the crank.

Let's keep it simple: the chain is a line from (170+10, 320) = (180, 320) to (310, 320). Hmm, the crank circle's radius 30 centered on (310,320): the chain line at y=320 is the tangent point at (310, 320)... hmm, actually a line from y=320 touching a circle of radius 30 centered at (310,320) — the point (310,320) is the center, so a line passing through the center isn't tangent. But visually in a side view of a bicycle, we typically draw the chain as a straight line along the horizontal axis connecting the rear hub and crank. This is fine and symmetric — it's a standard way to draw it. Actually the chain is a bit above the crank axis. But for simplicity, and given the user emphasized alignment (chain alignment), a horizontal line from (170+something, 320) to (310, 320) is clean and symmetric.
